title: Alone, not lonely
hookLine: being alone isn't loneliness; learn to be at ease by yourself (Discourses 3.13)
carry: someone you can live with is there

lines: LONELY AT A PARTY OF TWO HUNDRED.
AT EASE ON A QUIET WALK.
cards: A party of two hundred people can be lonelier than a quiet walk by yourself. Some people who live alone are deeply at ease, while some who are never alone feel stranded.
A full calendar doesn't promise company, and an empty room doesn't promise loneliness. Epictetus heard people in crowded Rome say they'd been left all alone.

teach.h: ALONE ISN'T THE SAME AS FORLORN.
teach.b: Discourses book three, chapter thirteen: what solitude is. Epictetus separates two things we usually blur.
Being alone doesn't make someone forlorn, any more than a crowd makes them not forlorn.

When we lose a brother, a child or a friend, we say we've been left all alone, even while living in Rome, with crowds in the street and neighbors on every side. So what is the forlorn feeling, really?
Being without help, he says: exposed, at the mercy of whatever comes. Then an image from Stoic belief about the cosmos.
In the Stoic picture he's drawing on, the world goes through cycles, and at the end of each it's drawn back into fire. In that moment, Zeus is alone. Yet he isn't forlorn.

teach.h: ZEUS ALONE, AT REST WITH HIMSELF.
teach.b: He's at rest with himself, thinking about how things are ordered. We should be able to do something like that: talk with ourselves, be at peace without needing others, not be lost when there's no one to fill the hours.

teach.h: A PEACE NO EMPEROR CAN GIVE.
teach.b: The emperor gives the world a great peace: no wars, no pirates, safe roads.

But he can't give peace from fever, shipwreck, grief or envy. That inner peace has to be learned. One of its first lessons is sitting in an empty room and finding that someone you can live with is there.

how: Some people drawn to Stoicism set aside a short time each day to be alone without distractions, treating it as practice in being at ease with themselves.

o: lonely, the ache of missing other people
by yourself, which isn't the same as forlorn
cut off and without help from anyone

games.q: alone, not lonely: tap the pairs.
p: alone and at rest with himself
no wars, no pirates, safe roads

s: Epictetus says being alone is the same as being lonely
he separates them: forlorn means being without help, not being by yourself.
he says the emperor can't give peace from grief or envy
the emperor gives peace from war; inner peace has to be learned.
in the Stoic picture, Zeus is alone when the world returns to fire
and he is at rest with himself, not forlorn.

games.q: a student has lost a close friend and says: now I'm all alone, though he lives in crowded Rome. what does Epictetus point out?
o: being alone and being forlorn aren't the same; you can learn to be at ease with yourself.
games.why: he says the forlorn feeling is being without help, and that we can learn to keep ourselves company, the way Zeus is at rest when alone.

practice: Sit somewhere you can be by yourself, even a corner, and notice whether being alone feels restful, a little uneasy, or both. Without reaching for your phone, ask yourself gently, the way a friend would: how are you, really?
Listen, and let the quiet be enough for a while.

wordCard.voice: Alone. Epictetus on solitude: being by yourself isn't the same as being forlorn, and we can learn to be at ease in our own company.

orig.note: Greek erēmia: solitude, desolation (our word hermit comes from the same root); the subject of Discourses 3.13.

carryVoice: Your line: someone you can live with is there. Being by yourself and being forlorn are two different things. That's day four hundred twenty-one.

sources.ref: Discourses 3.13 (what solitude is, and what kind of person a solitary is)
